title: Why Russia and Japan Never Made Peace After World War Two
voice: platform narration voice — selected in chat

paragraphs.scene: HOOK — THE WAR THAT NEVER GOT A TREATY
paragraphs.text: World War Two ended in the Pacific in nineteen forty-five. Japan surrendered. Soviet forces occupied a chain of islands north of Hokkaido. Yet Russia and Japan still have no formal peace treaty. This is not a war with armies facing each other across a trench. It is a war whose legal ending became trapped in four islands, several names, and a line drawn through cold water. To understand why the treaty never came, we have to follow that line from the nineteenth century to the present day.

The Kuril chain curves northeast from Japan toward Russia's Kamchatka Peninsula. At its southern end, a short span of sea separates Hokkaido from islands known in Japan as the Northern Territories and in Russia as the Southern Kurils. The names are not neutral labels. They reveal two different historical stories. Japan identifies Etorofu, Kunashiri, Shikotan, and the Habomai group as four islands that should be returned. Russia administers the islands as part of its Far Eastern territory. The map is small at this scale. The consequences have never been small.

paragraphs.scene: A BORDER BEFORE THE EMPIRES COLLIDED
paragraphs.text: The first important line was agreed in eighteen fifty-five. The Treaty of Shimoda placed the boundary between Etorofu and Urup. In the treaty text, Etorofu was Japanese and Urup, together with the islands north of it, was Russian. Kunashiri, Shikotan, and Habomai lay south of Etorofu. For Japan, this early border is central evidence that the four disputed islands were historically separate from the Kuril chain. For the later Russian and Soviet story, the decisive chapter came after a far larger war. Both memories begin with real documents. They simply give different documents the final word.

Twenty years later, another bargain redrew the northern map. In eighteen seventy-five, Japan received the rest of the Kuril chain, while Russia gained undisputed control of Sakhalin. The arrangement made the chain look straightforward for a time: Japan extended north through the islands, and Russia held Sakhalin. But treaties are snapshots, not permanent weather. The balance of power in Northeast Asia changed rapidly. When Russia and Japan fought in nineteen oh four and nineteen oh five, the peace settlement gave Japan the southern half of Sakhalin. The map became a record of victories as well as agreements.

paragraphs.scene: THE SECOND WORLD WAR CHANGES EVERYTHING
paragraphs.text: In the final weeks of World War Two, the old map broke again. Allied wartime planning included an agreement at Yalta that the Kuril Islands would be handed to the Soviet Union after the Soviet entry into the war against Japan. In August nineteen forty-five, the Soviet Union declared war on Japan and moved into the Kurils. General Order Number One, issued on September second under Allied command, directed Japanese forces in the Kurils to surrender to the Soviet commander in the Far East. Soviet control of the island chain followed. What had been a frontier of treaties now became a contested question of the postwar settlement.

paragraphs.scene: FOUR ISLANDS, TWO NAMES, ONE GAP
paragraphs.text: The four southern islands did not disappear from the argument. Japan calls them Etorofu, Kunashiri, Shikotan, and Habomai. Russian usage commonly names the larger islands Iturup and Kunashir and treats the group as part of the Southern Kurils. Japan says the four are not included in the Kurils it renounced after the war. Russia says the postwar outcome established its sovereignty over the islands. This film does not decide a sovereignty claim. It shows why a peace treaty is difficult: each side begins with a different boundary, a different legal reading, and a different name for the same shore.

The next obstacle arrived in nineteen fifty-one. Under the San Francisco Peace Treaty, Japan renounced rights, title, and claim to the Kuril Islands and to southern Sakhalin that it had gained after the Russo-Japanese War. The Soviet Union did not sign that treaty. The text did not end the disagreement over the four southern islands. Japan argues that they were not part of the Kurils covered by its renunciation. The Soviet and later Russian position treats the postwar territorial outcome differently. A treaty meant to settle the Pacific war left the most sensitive line on this map unresolved.

These islands are not merely dots on a diplomatic map. They sit beside the approaches to the Sea of Okhotsk, near rich fishing waters and on the route between Hokkaido and the Russian Far East. Their position gives them strategic meaning as well as emotional meaning. But geography alone does not explain the stalemate. Many states share difficult coastlines and still sign treaties. Here, geography became inseparable from the memory of defeat, the legacy of empire, and the question of whether a postwar boundary can ever be reopened without changing the story of the war itself.

paragraphs.scene: NINETEEN FIFTY-SIX: PEACE, BUT NOT A PEACE TREATY
paragraphs.text: In nineteen fifty-six, Moscow and Tokyo found a partial way forward. Their Joint Declaration ended the state of war and restored diplomatic relations. It also said that the two governments would continue negotiations for a peace treaty. Article Nine added a crucial promise: after a peace treaty, the Soviet Union would hand over Habomai and Shikotan to Japan. That formula reopened embassies and ended the formal state of war. But it did not settle Etorofu and Kunashiri. The document was a bridge across the diplomatic gap, not the final bridge across the water.

paragraphs.scene: WHY THE COMPROMISE DID NOT CLOSE THE CASE
paragraphs.text: The declaration’s conditional language contained its own problem. Habomai and Shikotan would be transferred only after a peace treaty. Japan continued to seek a settlement involving all four islands. Soviet and Russian approaches treated the issue differently, and the wider Cold War made compromise harder rather than easier. The dispute was therefore not frozen because nobody tried to talk. It remained alive because every possible formula answered one question while reopening another. Which islands were being discussed? Which treaty mattered most? And would a concession settle the border, or only create the next argument?

When the Soviet Union dissolved in nineteen ninety-one, Russia inherited the islands and the unfinished negotiations. In nineteen ninety-three, the Tokyo Declaration identified Etorofu, Kunashiri, Shikotan, and Habomai as the islands at issue and set a goal of resolving their attribution before concluding a peace treaty. That mattered because it put the four names into a shared diplomatic text. It did not erase the different legal positions beneath them. The new Russia and post-Cold War Japan could speak more openly, yet they still faced the same dilemma inherited from nineteen forty-five and nineteen fifty-six.

For a time, leaders explored whether the nineteen fifty-six declaration could become a basis for a final settlement. But trust depends on more than a map. Domestic politics, security concerns, and the broader relationship between Russia, Japan, and the United States shaped every negotiation. After Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Japan joined sanctions, and Russia announced in March twenty twenty-two that it would no longer continue peace-treaty negotiations with Japan. In February twenty twenty-six, the Kremlin said relations with Japan had been reduced to zero and no peace dialogue was under way. Then, in August twenty twenty-six, Vladimir Putin made his first visit to the Kuril Islands, landing on Iturup, the island Japan calls Etorofu. Japan's prime minister called the visit unacceptable. The old dispute had become entangled with a new crisis.

Saying that Russia and Japan have no peace treaty can sound as if the Second World War is still being fought. It is not. The nineteen fifty-six declaration ended the state of war and restored diplomatic relations. Both countries still maintain diplomatic relations and embassies, even when contacts are strained. The missing treaty has a narrower but powerful meaning. It would be the document intended to close the territorial question and place the postwar relationship on a final legal foundation. The fighting ended. The settlement did not.

paragraphs.scene: WHY FOUR ISLANDS CAN HOLD SO MUCH HISTORY
paragraphs.text: The islands matter because they compress a century and a half into a few volcanic shores. They hold the memory of the first Russia-Japan border, the exchange of Sakhalin for the Kurils, the shocks of two wars, the collapse of empire, and the unfinished language of nineteen fifty-six. On a map, the line may seem easy to draw. In diplomacy, every version of that line says something about what happened before it. That is why a small island group can resist a solution for generations.

So why did Russia and Japan never make peace after World War Two? Because the war ended with a map that both sides read differently. The Soviet occupation in nineteen forty-five, the wording of the nineteen fifty-one treaty, and the unfinished promise of nineteen fifty-six created a problem that no later negotiation could easily escape. Russia controls the islands. Japan maintains its claim. And between Hokkaido and Kamchatka, a narrow chain of land still carries an unfinished line from the last world war.
